lines.text: I
Joy! light! Who does not wish it for himself! Of course at
a time like the present we feel very strongly that it must be
no ordinary joy—not the kind of rejoicing in which we might
forget what is happening around us and with us, no joy
which might lull us into forgetfulness of the heavy hardships
we are undergoing, hardships which forbid all frivolous
delights, no joy which would drown our remembrance of
those who are fighting for us, and in face of whom we at
home ask ourselves the question whether we have any right
to rejoice at all, or to wish joy for ourselves. No! it must be
no ordinary joy but it must at least be a joy which we would
share in common with our fighting men, and which would
link us with them. But in any case it cannot be joy of an
ordinary kind. For how could any ordinary joy last in face
of the distresses of the time? Such joy would be no more than
the frivolous pleasures of two or three fleeting days, after
which all would seem dark again around us and within us.
No, it can be no ordinary joy! It would at least have to be
a joy which had the power to predominate over anxiety and
grief, and to become within us a living source of power to
transform the darkness around and within into light. No
ordinary joy, which again means no joy such as earthly
things confer. It would have to be eternal supernatural joy.
And this is what it is to be! The message of Christmas speaks
of precisely such a joy; and for this heavenly joy are we to
prepare ourselves in the season of Advent. We are to move
towards an encounter with Him who wishes us to come to
Him, and who says: "I am the light of the world. He who
follows me will not walk in darkness but will have the light
of life."
"The light of life"-what is the meaning of that? What
does Jesus promise the one who follows Him? What are we
to picture to ourselves as the meaning of the phrase, "light
of life"? To be frank, we can form no clear idea of what it
means. But that very fact suggests simply that the gift of
